title: 1982–1987: A New Historical High
tagline: Supply-side victory · Escape from stagflation · Plaza Accord · America's Second Revolution

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: When Reagan took office, the Volcker tightening and the second oil crisis had pushed the US economy into its deepest postwar recession. But the supply-side policy mix — tax cuts, deregulation, monetary control, and spending restraint — made 1982 the end of stagflation: CPI fell from 10.3% in 1981 to 6.2% in 1982, and to just 1.9% by 1986.

Then came the 'golden five years': from 1983 through 1987 the US economy expanded steadily, and the NBER identified no recessions in this stretch. Unemployment fell from a peak of 10.8% in 1982 to 5.4% in 1987. America had reached a new high — leaving thirteen years of stagflation behind.

But these years also sowed structural imbalances: cutting taxes without cutting spending produced the 'twin deficits' (trade and fiscal); a strong dollar crushed exports, leading to the deliberate devaluation under the 1985 Plaza Accord; and financialization accelerated, setting up the late-1980s junk-bond and S&L crises. Black Monday in 1987 — a one-day decline of 20.5% — was a reminder of the fragility built into financial engineering.

items.body: 1982 GDP was −1.8%, with Q1 at −2.2% — the cost of stacking the second oil crisis on top of the Volcker tightening. But inflation was finally tamed: 1982 CPI came in at 6.2% (down four points from 10.3% the year before). Monetary policy turned easier in 1983 and GDP rebounded to 4.6% (Q4 at 7.9%).

items.strong: 1984–1985: Trade Deficits and the Plaza Accord
items.body: 1984 GDP was +7.2%, but the strong dollar crushed exports and the trade deficit widened to 3% of GDP. On September 22, 1985, the G5 signed the Plaza Accord to coordinate a deliberate dollar depreciation. By year-end the dollar had fallen 16.6% against the yen.

The Fed cut rates four times for a total of 200bp in 1986 and consumer spending held up. The Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86) was signed on September 27; Reagan called it 'America's Second Revolution' — the top individual rate from 50% to 28%, top corporate rate from 46% to 34%, and broad simplification. The economy grew 3.5% in 1987, but the S&P 500 fell 20.5% in a single day on Black Monday in October.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: From Industry to Services
body: Manufacturing offshoring accelerated. Manufacturing's share of total US corporate profits fell from 40.8% in 1981 to 28.9% in 1987 — nearly 12 points in five years. Overseas profits' share, by contrast, rose from 14.4% to 22.0%, as US multinationals moved production abroad while still booking the earnings at home.

Finance and real estate stood toe to toe with manufacturing for the first time: in 1987 it reached 18% of GDP, tied with manufacturing in the top tier. This was the inflection point at which the US shifted from a manufacturing-led economy to a finance-led one.

Internal differentiation within services accelerated: business services, education and health, and utilities led with annualized nominal growth of 11.8%, 10.6%, and 9.8%, while manufacturing managed only 5.2% and mining ran at −8.2% (hit by the oil-price collapse). Primary metals, machinery, and other traditional heavy industries entered prolonged decline.

Macro and micro diverged again: from 1982 to 1987 nominal GDP grew 51.4%, but cumulative pre-tax corporate profits rose only 19.6% and after-tax profits 5.7% — the effective tax rate rebounded from 28% in 1985 to 35% in 1986, eroding reported earnings.

sections.heading: Taxes: Two Major Reagan-Era Reforms
body: The Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA, August 1981): top individual rate from 70% to 50%, expanded accelerated depreciation, and capital gains from 28% to 20%. Reagan's first round of cuts.

The Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86, September 1986): Reagan called this America's Second Revolution. The principle was 'broad base, low rates, simple code': individual brackets were collapsed from fourteen ranging from 11%–50% down to just 15% and 28%; the top corporate rate moved from 46% to 34%; corporate capital-gains preferences were eliminated; and various loopholes for the wealthy and corporations were closed to broaden the base and keep the package revenue-neutral.

items.body: On August 13, Mexico announced it could not service its foreign debt, followed by Brazil and Argentina. Major US banks (Citibank, Chase) took a serious hit.
items.title: Latin American Debt Crisis

items.body: Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), escalating the Cold War arms race.
items.title: Star Wars Initiative

items.body: On September 22, finance ministers from the US, Japan, Germany, France, and the UK met at New York's Plaza Hotel and agreed on a coordinated dollar depreciation.
items.title: Plaza Accord

items.body: MS-DOS and IBM PC compatibles spread rapidly; the personal computer industry took off.
items.title: IBM/Microsoft Partnership

items.body: On January 28, the shuttle broke apart 73 seconds after launch; seven astronauts were killed and the US human spaceflight program was suspended.
items.title: Challenger Disaster

items.body: Soviet nuclear disaster, and the US 'Operation El Dorado Canyon' airstrikes on Libya.
items.title: Chernobyl and Libya Airstrikes

items.body: Reagan signed the Tax Reform Act on September 27.
items.title: TRA86 Signed

items.body: In early November, a Lebanese magazine exposed covert US arms sales to Iran, sparking a major political crisis for the Reagan administration. That same month, junk-bond king Michael Milken was indicted for securities fraud.
items.title: Iran-Contra and Milken Indicted

items.body: On February 22, the G6 signed the Louvre Accord in Paris to stabilize exchange rates and halt the excess dollar depreciation triggered by the Plaza Accord.
items.title: Louvre Accord

items.body: On August 11, Alan Greenspan succeeded Volcker, beginning an eighteen-year tenure.
items.title: Greenspan Becomes Fed Chair

items.body: The S&P 500 fell 20.5% in a single day and the Dow 22.6% — record one-day declines. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 33.33% on October 26.
items.title: Black Monday
